name: Metchnikoff's thorn and the standing army
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: How the body's fast, always-on defence was discovered — and why it is a separate army from the antibody one. T1: Messina, Sicily, 1882 — Elie Metchnikoff, a Russian zoologist on holiday, was watching transparent starfish larvae; he pushed a garden thorn into one and sat up all night, and by morning a crowd of wandering cells had gathered around the splinter and was engulfing it (the hook: the animal was see-through, so he could WATCH the defence happen). T2: he named the eating cells 'phagocytes' — devouring cells, a term his Vienna colleague Carl Claus suggested — and made the claim that turned medicine around: inflammation, the redness and heat and swelling every doctor treated as the disease, is the BATTLE, not the damage. T3: the resistance — the reigning humoral school held that immunity lived in the fluids of the blood, not in cells, and that white cells merely carried germs around; Emil von Behring and much of the bacteriological establishment dismissed him, and Rudolf Virchow was his key defender. T4: the 1908 Nobel Prize settled it by refusing to choose — Metchnikoff (cells) shared it with Paul Ehrlich (antibodies in serum), and the modern division into INNATE immunity (fast, general, no memory) and ADAPTIVE immunity (slow, exquisitely specific, remembers) grew out of that truce. T5 (mechanism): innate immunity turned out to have a recognition system of its own — Charles Janeway argued in 1989 that innate cells must carry receptors tuned to patterns shared by whole classes of microbe; Jules Hoffmann showed in 1996 (Cell) that fruit flies with a broken Toll gene died of fungal infection, and Bruce Beutler found that mice unable to respond to bacterial endotoxin had a broken TLR4 — Janeway's predicted receptor, found. Nobel 2011. Further rungs: (a) Ralph Steinman's 1973 discovery of the dendritic cell (Journal of Experimental Medicine, with Zanvil Cohn), the branched cell that carries a captured fragment from the innate front line to the adaptive specialists — the bridge between the two armies; Steinman later treated his own pancreatic cancer with dendritic-cell therapies of his own design and died on 30 September 2011, three days before the Nobel committee named him, which awarded the prize anyway. (b) Metchnikoff tested his own gut theory by DRINKING a culture of cholera during the 1892 French epidemic and stayed well, while a colleague who drank the same culture nearly died. (c) Complement — the heat-sensitive killing activity in fresh serum that Hans Buchner found in 1890 — is the innate half of the humoral side, and punches holes in bacterial membranes.
source: Wikipedia 'Elie Metchnikoff' (1882 Messina starfish-larva thorn experiment; Claus coined 'phagocyte'; Virchow's support; von Behring/humoral opposition; 1908 Nobel shared with Ehrlich; 1892 cholera self-experiment); Wikipedia 'Toll-like receptor' (Nusslein-Volhard's 1985 'Das ist ja toll!'; Hoffmann 1996 Cell, Toll and antifungal peptides; Beutler's positional cloning of TLR4 as the LPS sensor; Janeway and Medzhitov 1997; Beutler and Hoffmann share the 2011 Nobel); Wikipedia 'Ralph M. Steinman' (1973 dendritic cells with Zanvil Cohn, J Exp Med 137(5); named for their dendrites; died 30 Sept 2011, prize announced 3 Oct 2011, committee let the award stand). NOTE: grokipedia.com returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch for the Mechnikov page this session — the build's research stage must run the Grokipedia check on 'Ilya Mechnikov', 'Innate immune system' and 'Ralph Steinman' before authoring.
framing_note: DISCOVERY-anchored opener for the whole sub-strand, closing on MECHANISM. T1 keys the SCENE — a see-through larva, a thorn, an all-night vigil — never 'who discovered phagocytosis'. ACCURACY RAIL (the one that matters): sources disagree on the thorn. Wikipedia says citrus thorns; the family memoir tradition says rose thorns from the garden. Write it as 'a garden thorn' and NEVER put the plant in the tested slot. Second rail: Metchnikoff was a zoologist on holiday, not a physician at a bedside — that is part of the wonder. Teach-before-test: 'innate' and 'adaptive' must be explained in a stem before any rung tests the distinction. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real losing/rival science of the humoral school — antitoxin in serum, Ehrlich's side-chain theory, Behring's diphtheria antitoxin, Buchner's alexin — all respectable, all partly right, which is exactly the point. Dinner-test payoff: T1, plus the cholera-beaker rung (a self-test that rhymes with Barry Marshall and should be cross-referenced in build, not duplicated). LANE BORDER: the starfish larva is laboratory EQUIPMENT here, not natural history — ANIMAL bank owns echinoderm biology; SCIENCE owns the cell-defence discovery.

name: Miller's thymus and Glick's chickens
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: The two accidents that split the immune system into T cells and B cells. T1: 1961 — the thymus, a lump of tissue behind the breastbone that shrinks as you grow, sat in every anatomy textbook as a useless leftover. Jacques Miller, a young PhD student in London, cut it out of NEWBORN mice; those mice grew up unable to fight infection and unable to reject skin grafted from a completely different animal. An organ everyone had written off turned out to be running the defence system. T2: Miller published 'Immunological function of the thymus' in The Lancet on 30 September 1961, and is described as the last living scientist to have discovered the function of a human organ. The timing is the fact: remove the thymus from an ADULT mouse and little happens — it does its work early and then retires. T3: five years earlier, in a chicken barn at Ohio State, Bruce Glick had removed the bursa of Fabricius — a small pouch near the tail — from young birds and found nothing at all. Fellow graduate student Timothy Chang then borrowed Glick's birds for a routine classroom demonstration of antibody production against Salmonella; the birds made no antibody, and most of them died. The failed class demo WAS the experiment. T4: the resistance — Glick, Chang and George Jaap could not get the result into Science and published it in Poultry Science in 1956, where it became one of the most-cited papers that journal ever ran. The bursa is why they are called B cells; the thymus is why the others are T cells. T5: Miller and his student Graham Mitchell showed in 1967-68 (Nature) that the two lineages must COOPERATE — a B cell makes antibody only when a T cell gives it permission — so the immune system fires on a two-key launch rather than one, which is a large part of why it so rarely turns on you by accident. Further rungs: (a) mammals have no bursa, so human B cells mature in the bone marrow — the letter survived the organ. (b) DiGeorge syndrome, in which a child is born with little or no thymus, is the natural experiment that confirmed Miller's mouse result in humans.
source: Wikipedia 'Jacques Miller' (neonatal thymectomy in mice; 'Immunological function of the thymus', Lancet, 30 Sept 1961, 2(7205):748-749; thymus previously believed vestigial; T/B subsets with Graham Mitchell, Nature, 18 Nov 1967; 'only living person to have first described the functions of a human organ'); Wikipedia 'Bruce Glick' (bursa of Fabricius controls antibody production; Timothy Chang's borrowed birds; rejected by Science, published in Poultry Science 1956 as 'The Bursa of Fabricius and Antibody Production'; origin of the term 'B cells'). NOTE: the Wikipedia summary says GEESE while the standard immunology accounts say chickens (White Leghorn) — see accuracy rail.
framing_note: A DISCOVERY ladder built out of two accidents, which is its charm: neither man set out to find a lymphocyte lineage. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Miller's mice were thymectomised as NEWBORNS — the developmental window is the load-bearing fact and must not be blurred into 'he removed the thymus from mice'. (2) The bird species: Glick's 1956 Poultry Science work is standardly reported as chickens, but at least one encyclopaedia summary says geese — the build MUST settle this from the 1956 paper itself, and until it does, the bird species may not appear in the tested slot. DISTRACTOR MINE: real organs that were genuinely written off as vestigial (appendix, tonsils, spleen, pineal) and the real rival theories of the thymus (a growth gland, an endocrine gland, a fat store). Dinner-test payoff: T3 — a routine class demonstration accidentally discovered B cells and the answer was sitting in a barn. No stance anywhere in this ladder. LANE BORDER: the chicken is equipment, not ANIMAL-bank content; do not drift into poultry biology.

name: Tonegawa and the genome that cuts itself up
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: How a few thousand gene segments make more antibodies than there are stars in the galaxy — the gamble and the edit. T1: the arithmetic that broke immunology. Your body can build a matching antibody against a molecule that never existed on Earth until a chemist made it last week — yet you carry only about 20,000 genes in total. The wonder is the mismatch, not the number. T2: the answer everyone believed was that the invader itself acted as a MOULD — Linus Pauling's 1940 template theory had the antibody folding itself around the antigen like clay pressed onto a coin. It was elegant, it was wrong, and the man who was wrong was the best chemist alive. T3: Macfarlane Burnet's 1957 clonal selection theory flipped the logic — every lymphocyte is born committed to ONE shape, made blind, before any invader arrives; the antigen does not instruct, it merely SELECTS which cell is allowed to multiply. Gustav Nossal and Joshua Lederberg tested it in 1958 by isolating single cells: one cell, one antibody. T4: 1976, the Basel Institute for Immunology — Nobumichi Hozumi and Susumu Tonegawa cut DNA from mouse embryo cells and from antibody-making tumour cells with the same restriction enzyme and found the antibody gene pieces in DIFFERENT places in the two. The B cell had physically cut its own chromosome and stitched the pieces back together (PNAS 73:3628-3632, 1976; Nobel 1987). The dogma this destroyed: that every cell in your body carries an identical, unaltered copy of your genome. T5: the shuffle is only the gamble; the EDIT comes next. Once a B cell finds a rough match, it deliberately mutates its own antibody gene at an enormous rate inside a germinal centre, and the daughter cells compete for scarce antigen — a Darwinian tournament run inside your lymph node over days, ending with a key filed to fit a lock nobody designed it for. Further rungs: (a) William Dreyer and J. Claude Bennett proposed in 1965 that two separate genes made one antibody chain; it violated 'one gene, one protein' and was widely dismissed until Tonegawa proved it. (b) Junctional sloppiness — the enzyme TdT adds random letters where the segments are spliced, so joining the same three segments twice gives two different antibodies; most of the diversity comes from the untidiness of the joins, not the shuffle itself. (c) The same cutting enzymes, RAG1 and RAG2, are what make the rearrangement possible — and a child born without working RAG genes has no adaptive immunity at all.
source: Hozumi N, Tonegawa S, 'Evidence for somatic rearrangement of immunoglobulin genes coding for variable and constant regions', PNAS 1976;73(10):3628-3632 (BamHI digestion of BALB/c embryo DNA vs MOPC 321 plasmacytoma DNA, hybridised with labelled kappa V- and C-region probes; V and C genes distant in the embryo are joined into one contiguous stretch during lymphocyte differentiation); Wikipedia 'Susumu Tonegawa' (1987 Nobel, 'for his discovery of the genetic principle for generation of antibody diversity'); Wikipedia 'Clonal selection' (Jerne 1955; Talmage 1957; Burnet 1957 'A modification of Jerne's theory of antibody production using the concept of clonal selection', Australian Journal of Science; Nossal and Lederberg 1958 Nature, one B cell = one antibody); Wikipedia 'V(D)J recombination' (V/D/J segment counts for the human heavy chain; TdT adds non-templated N nucleotides; RAG1/RAG2).
framing_note: A MECHANISM ladder on a REVERSAL spine. The tested fact is always the MOVE — the cell edits its own DNA, the antigen selects rather than instructs — never a number to recite. ACCURACY RAIL (the one that matters): do NOT state a hard repertoire figure such as 'a billion antibodies from 20,000 genes'. Published estimates of the potential repertoire vary by orders of magnitude and Wikipedia's own 3x10^11 combinatorial figure is flagged as uncited; write the wonder as 'vastly more antibodies than genes' and admit any specific count only where the build can source it. Teach-before-test: 'gene segment', 'recombination' and 'mutation' must each be explained in a stem before a rung tests them. DISTRACTOR MINE: the graveyard of respectable-but-wrong immunology — Pauling's instructive/template theory, 'one gene, one protein', the idea that you inherit one gene per antibody, Ehrlich's side chains. Dinner-test payoff: T4 — the cells in your blood do not have the same genome as the cells in your arm, because they cut theirs up on purpose. LANE BORDER: the general DNA/gene/mutation machinery belongs to the genetics sub-strand of SCIENCE — every rung here must be keyed to the ANTIBODY problem, not to DNA in general.
history_overlap: Possible overlap with a SCIENCE genetics sub-strand on DNA, mutation and the central dogma — this ladder owns Tonegawa/Hozumi 1976, clonal selection and somatic hypermutation; a genetics ladder must not re-key 'cells edit their own DNA' to a different discoverer.

name: Horror autotoxicus: the self-or-other checkpoint and its failures
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: How the body learns what counts as 'me' — and what happens when the lesson fails. T1: cattle. Ray Owen found in 1945 that non-identical twin calves that had shared a placenta in the womb carried each other's red blood cells for the rest of their lives and never attacked them. Tolerance is not something you inherit; it is something you LEARN, and you learn it before you are born. T2: the dogma this cracked. Around 1901 Paul Ehrlich declared that the body possesses a 'horror autotoxicus' — a horror of self-poisoning — and is protected against attacking its own tissues. It became so authoritative that for fifty years doctors who saw an obvious self-attack looked for some other explanation instead. T3: Peter Medawar, Rupert Billingham and Leslie Brent turned Owen's cattle into a prediction and tested it in 1953 — inject newborn mice with cells from a different strain, and those mice grow up accepting skin grafts that any other mouse would tear off within days. Anything present while the system is being built gets filed as 'self'. Burnet and Medawar shared the 1960 Nobel Prize for acquired immunological tolerance. T4 (the reversal): in 1956, in Buffalo, Noel Rose injected rabbits with thyroid protein and watched the animals' own immune systems chew up their own thyroids — precisely the thing Ehrlich's rule said could not happen. His supervisor Ernst Witebsky, trained in Ehrlich's own tradition, made him repeat the experiment before he would believe it. T5 (mechanism): the thymus runs a lethal audition. Developing T cells are shown fragments of the body's own proteins, and any cell that binds its own body too tightly is killed on the spot; a gene called AIRE forces thymus cells to display proteins borrowed from organs all over the body, so that the audition can cover tissue the thymus itself will never meet. Further rungs: (a) molecular mimicry — after a strep throat, antibodies raised against the bacterium's M protein can cross-react with heart tissue, and the scarred valves of rheumatic fever are friendly fire; honest caveat, the mimicry account is still argued and no single culprit antigen has been formally pinned down. (b) Type 1 diabetes is the checkpoint failing on one cell type: the immune system destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas, which is why it is not a disease of eating wrongly. (c) In lupus the antibodies are aimed at DNA itself, which is why the disease can appear anywhere in the body at once. (d) The open mystery: roughly four in five autoimmune patients are women, and lupus runs about nine to one female; being female is the single largest known risk factor for autoimmune disease, and nobody yet knows why.
source: Wikipedia 'Immunological tolerance' (Owen 1945, dizygotic twin cattle sharing a placenta and a stable mixture of each other's red cells; Medawar, Billingham and Brent 1953, foreign cells injected into fetal/neonatal mice produce later graft acceptance; Burnet and Fenner first propose deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes; Burnet and Medawar share the 1960 Nobel for 'the discovery of acquired immune tolerance'); Wikipedia 'Autoimmunity' (Ehrlich's horror autotoxicus at the turn of the 20th century and its authoritative status; the 1904 paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria finding that it suppressed; Noel Rose and Ernst Witebsky in New York, Roitt and Doniach at UCL; molecular mimicry via Group A streptococci with no antigen formally identified in half a century; Hashimoto's 10:1 and SLE 9:1 female ratios; 'being female is the single greatest risk factor...yet discovered'); Wikipedia 'Noel Rose' (1950s rabbit thyroglobulin work at the University at Buffalo, first demonstration of autoimmunity).
framing_note: A CONCEPT/THEME ladder — one idea (self versus other) deepened across named cases — carrying a REVERSAL at T4 and a genuine MYSTERY at the top. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) State Ehrlich fairly. He did not claim autoantibodies were literally impossible; he allowed they could form and argued that regulatory mechanisms prevented harm. Write it that way or the rung is a straw man. (2) The Rose/Witebsky specifics — whether the thyroglobulin came from the rabbit's own gland or from other rabbits, and the exact 1956 journal — must be verified against the primary paper before authoring; the fact to key is that a SELF protein caused SELF damage. (3) On the female preponderance, say 'no one yet knows' proudly and make sure no distractor is secretly the truth. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival explanations serious doctors held — a hidden infection lurking in the organ, a toxin, 'nerves' and stress, heredity alone, and Ehrlich's own rule. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (twin calves swap blood before birth and stay friends for life) and T4 (the supervisor who refused to believe his own student's result). LANE BORDER: the calves and rabbits are instruments, not ANIMAL-bank content; and 'what is the self' as a philosophical question belongs to PHILOSOPHY — this ladder stays strictly cellular.

name: Natural immunity: the oldest measured fact in medicine
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: That surviving an infection leaves lasting protection is one of the best-attested facts in all of biology — measured for two and a half thousand years, and quietly unmentionable for about two. T1: Athens, 430 BC. Writing about the plague destroying his own city — a plague he caught and survived — Thucydides recorded that the sick were nursed by people who had already had the disease, because the same man was never attacked twice, or at least never fatally. The first written record of immunity was made by a historian, not a doctor. T2: the Faroe Islands, 1846. Measles reached the islands after an absence of about sixty-five years and swept through nearly the whole population — but the old people who had lived through the 1781 epidemic were untouched. A 25-year-old Danish physician, Peter Ludvig Panum, sent out to investigate, used that untouched group to establish that measles immunity lasts a lifetime, and pinned the incubation period at about a fortnight. T3 (mechanism): why it lasts. When the fight ends most of the army is stood down, but a small garrison of memory B and T cells survives for decades, and long-lived plasma cells park in the bone marrow and keep dribbling out antibody for years. That garrison is why a second exposure is finished before you ever feel it. T4: natural infection presents the WHOLE organism to the immune system — every protein, entering by the route the pathogen actually uses — so the resulting memory is broad and often includes the mucous membranes where the bug lands. Breadth is why some natural immunity survives the pathogen changing its coat. T5 (the stance rung): natural immunity was foundational, measured, textbook immunology for a century — and in 2020-21 a great deal of public messaging proceeded as though it did not exist or could not be counted. It was then measured directly: a 2023 Lancet systematic review and meta-analysis found protection from prior infection against severe disease remained high (of the order of 88 per cent at 40 weeks), and a January 2022 CDC MMWR report on California and New York found that during the Delta wave case rates were lowest among people with a previous infection. The lesson is the whole bank in one line: an institution can stop mentioning a fact without the fact changing. T5b (the honest caveat, mandatory): natural immunity is not free. The Faroese paid for theirs — more than a hundred islanders died. And measles buys its lifelong immunity to itself by wiping out immune memory to OTHER pathogens for up to three years, the 'immune amnesia' documented by Michael Mina and colleagues. Both things are true at once, and the ladder says both.
source: Wikipedia 'Measles' (Panum's 1846 Faroe Islands investigation; measles absent about 60 years so almost no acquired immunity remained; three-quarters of residents fell ill and more than 100, i.e. 1-2 per cent, died; Panum elucidated the immunity conferred by illness and the incubation period; Michael Mina's immune-amnesia work — measles-induced immune suppression lasting up to three years, memory lymphocytes destroyed); Wikipedia 'Peter Ludvig Panum' (aged 25 in 1846; 'Observations Made During the Epidemic of Measles on the Faroe Islands in the Year 1846'); Grokipedia 'Herd immunity' (natural infection engages the full antigenic repertoire including conserved nucleocapsid targets absent from some vaccines; a cited study finding reinfection risk 92 per cent lower after natural infection; measles natural infection yielding lifelong immunity in nearly all survivors; and the article's own note on institutional tendencies to discount natural contributions). NOTE: the Lancet 2023 meta-analysis and the Jan 2022 CDC MMWR (mm7104e1) both returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch this session — the build MUST retrieve both at source and verify the figures before any rung is written.
framing_note: STANCE LADDER — vision_mandated. The stance is factual rather than partisan: natural immunity is real, measured, and was uncontroversial pre-2020 textbook material, and its 2020-era dismissal was a failure of institutions, not of evidence. RAILS: (1) The load-bearing rungs are HISTORICAL — Thucydides, Panum, the memory-cell mechanism. Confine the stance to T5, key it to the EVIDENCE and the MESSAGING, and never name a living official or attach it to any vaccine recommendation. (2) Never imply 'therefore do not vaccinate' — the bank presents, it does not prescribe — and the immune-amnesia/death-toll caveat rung is REQUIRED so the ladder is honest in both directions. (3) Panum reported that the islanders who had had measles in 1781 were all spared and gave a count of them; the exact number could not be verified this session, so it may NOT appear in a stem until the build checks his 1847 treatise. Same rule for the Lancet 88 per cent and the MMWR rate ratios — verify at source or do not use them. (4) The Thucydides line must be given as a translation of his own words, attributed, and short. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival explanations of why some people were spared — miasma, humoral imbalance, 'constitution', divine favour, and the real modern competitors (waning, variant escape, hybrid immunity). Dinner-test payoff: T2 — the only people on the island who did not get sick were the ones old enough to remember 1781.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank may cover the Plague of Athens and the Peloponnesian War as an episode — this ladder keys ONLY Thucydides' observation that survivors were not struck twice, never the war, Pericles' death, or Athenian politics. Any SCIENCE vaccine/medicine sub-strand must not re-key the same 2020-era evidence rung.

name: Herd immunity, honestly
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: The threshold idea, where it came from, what it really assumes, and how it gets abused from both sides. T1: the phrase began literally, in a barnyard. American veterinary scientists were using 'herd immunity' about actual herds from the 1890s — Daniel Salmon in 1894 about the hardiness of well-fed hogs, and by 1916 Bureau of Animal Industry researchers about cattle that had recovered from brucellosis. It was a farmer's observation before it was an equation. T2: 1923, London — William Topley and Graham Wilson deliberately ran epidemics through cages of mice and showed that you do not have to make every animal immune to stop an outbreak. That is the moment herd immunity became an experimental fact instead of a figure of speech. T3: 1930s Baltimore — A. W. Hedrich went through decades of city measles records and found the pattern in the data: once enough of the city's children had already had measles, new cases fell away even among children who had never had it. Protection you receive without possessing it. T4 (mechanism): the threshold. If one case infects R-nought others in a wholly susceptible crowd, transmission dies out once the immune fraction passes one minus one over R-nought. Measles, with an R-nought around 12 to 18, needs roughly 92 to 95 per cent; a disease with an R-nought of 1.3 needs about 23 per cent. One fraction explains why measles is the hard case and influenza is not. The mathematical parent is Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 threshold theorem. T5 (the honest rung): the formula assumes things that are not true of real people. It assumes everyone mixes at random — real populations are clustered networks, and a 95 per cent national average can hide a 60 per cent neighbourhood. It assumes immunity is sterilising and permanent — much of it wanes, and much of it stops illness without stopping transmission. It assumes the pathogen does not evolve away from the immunity. Where those assumptions break, a population can pass the calculated threshold and still have outbreaks, which is not a paradox but a violated premise. T5b: OVERSHOOT. An epidemic left to run does not stop at the threshold; infections already in flight keep landing after transmission has turned over, so the final number infected overshoots the minimum, sometimes by a large fraction of the population. The threshold is where the curve turns, not where it stops. T5c: the concept has been abused in both directions in public argument — used to suggest a fixed magic number that ends an epidemic forever once crossed, and used to suggest that letting a disease run through a population is a strategy. The honest version is narrower and duller than either, and its value is precisely that it comes with a list of assumptions you are obliged to check.
source: Grokipedia 'Herd immunity' (p_c = 1 - 1/R0; measles R0 approx 12-18 giving 92-95 per cent; SARS-CoV-2 early R0 approx 2-3 giving 67-75 per cent; influenza R0 approx 1.3 giving about 23 per cent; Kermack and McKendrick 1927 'A Contribution to the Mathematical Theory of Epidemics' and the SIR threshold theorem; overshoot dynamics with final size s_inf = exp(-R0(1 - s_inf)) and overshoot of 20-30 per cent of the population at R0 = 3; homogeneous-mixing, sterilising-immunity and no-evolution assumptions; heterogeneity and waning elevating the effective threshold); Wikipedia 'Herd immunity' (term first used in 1894 by Daniel Elmer Salmon of the Bureau of Animal Industry about well-fed hogs; 1916 BIA usage for recovered cattle; 1923 British bacteriologists' mouse epidemics; A. W. Hedrich's 1930s Baltimore measles work; the four stated assumptions; the free-rider problem).
framing_note: The ANALYTIC BACKBONE of this sub-strand — a CONCEPT ladder with a native T4/T5 ceiling. vision_mandated because the stance IS the topic: the bank refuses both rhetorical abuses and teaches the assumptions instead of a slogan. RAILS: (1) TEACH BEFORE TEST — R-nought must be defined in plain words inside a stem before any rung tests the threshold formula, and the formula stays arithmetic (grade-10 ceiling: name Kermack and McKendrick, never put a differential equation in a stem). (2) The abuse rung at T5c must attach to the ASSUMPTION being violated, never to a named living person, a country, or a policy recommendation. (3) Do not let the ladder settle into 'herd immunity is fake' either — Hedrich's Baltimore data are real and the threshold is a genuine result; the honest position is that it is a model with premises. DISTRACTOR MINE: real epidemiological quantities that are NOT the threshold — case fatality rate, attack rate, R effective, incubation period, secondary attack rate — plus the real historical claimants to the term. Dinner-test payoff: T1/T2 — the phrase was coined about actual herds of hogs and cattle, and proved on cages of mice. LANE BORDER: MATH owns fractions and exponentials as arithmetic; here the formula is a claim about a real disease, not an algebra exercise.
history_overlap: Any SCIENCE germ-theory or epidemics sub-strand must not re-key Topley and Wilson 1923 or Hedrich's Baltimore measles data — this ladder owns them. The 'natural immunity' ladder owns the 2020-era evidence rung; this one must not repeat it.

name: Strachan's siblings and the Amish barn
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: Why allergies climb as childhoods get cleaner — presented as the serious, well-supported, still-incomplete hypothesis it is. T1: 1989, London. David Strachan went looking for the cause of hay fever in a study that had followed more than 17,000 British children born in a single week of March 1958. The strongest thing in the data was not pollen, not pollution, not smoking. It was how many OLDER brothers and sisters a child had — the more older siblings, the less hay fever, with firstborns worst off. T2: his explanation — big families pass infections around, and something in that early microbial traffic teaches the immune system not to overreact later on. Note carefully what he did NOT say: he did not say washing causes allergies. 'Hygiene' here is shorthand for a shrunken microbial world — smaller families, clean water, fewer animals, more antibiotics, more time indoors. T3 (the natural experiment that is very hard to explain away): Amish and Hutterite children in the American Midwest share ancestry, diet, family size, low smoking and a farming life — but the Amish keep single-family dairy farms with children in and out of the barns, while the Hutterites farm industrially and keep children away from the animals. In a 2016 New England Journal of Medicine study led by Michelle Stein, asthma was about four times less common and allergic sensitisation about six times less common among the Amish children, and Amish house dust carried far more bacterial endotoxin. T4 (the step from correlation to cause): the same team took house dust from Amish and Hutterite homes and put it into the airways of mice. Mice given Amish dust were protected against an asthma-like response; mice given Hutterite dust were not — and the protection vanished in mice whose innate-immune signalling was broken. The dust itself was doing it, through the innate system. T5 (mechanism): the training runs through regulatory T cells. Gut bacteria fermenting dietary fibre release short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, which push naive T cells toward the Foxp3-positive regulatory type — the cells whose whole job is to say 'stand down, this is harmless'. Fewer microbes, fewer brakes, and an immune system that treats birch pollen as an invasion. T5b (refinement and the honest limits): Graham Rook's 2003 'Old Friends' version argues that it is not childhood INFECTIONS that protect but lifelong companions — soil bacteria, gut commensals, helminth worms — that we co-evolved with, which is why farm life and pet ownership protect while a bout of RSV in infancy makes asthma WORSE. And the limits must be stated: not every microbe protects, the extension from allergy to autoimmune disease is far weaker than the allergy evidence, and confounders like pollution, diet and genetics are not fully separated. A strong hypothesis, not a closed case.
source: Grokipedia 'Hygiene hypothesis' (Strachan 1989; British National Child Development Study, over 16,000 individuals born in March 1958; inverse association between hay fever at 23 and number of older siblings, strongest effect in firstborns; 'hygiene' explicitly not literal cleanliness; Graham Rook's 'Old Friends' hypothesis circa 2003 and co-evolved immunoregulatory microbes; SCFAs, butyrate and propionate acting via GPR43/GPR109A and HDAC inhibition to promote Foxp3 and Treg differentiation; germ-free mice needing diverse colonisation for colonic Treg restoration; RSV as a counter-example infection that worsens allergy; stated criticisms and confounders); Stein MM et al., 'Innate Immunity and Asthma Risk in Amish and Hutterite Farm Children', N Engl J Med 2016 Aug 4;375(5):411-421, PMID 27518660 (asthma and allergic sensitisation 4x and 6x lower in the Amish despite similar genetic ancestry and lifestyle; higher endotoxin in Amish house dust; protection operating through innate immune pathways). CAUTION: Grokipedia's own article contradicts itself on the cohort, naming the 1958 NCDS in one section and the 1970 British Cohort Study in another — see accuracy rail.
framing_note: The model DISCOVERY -> NATURAL-EXPERIMENT -> CAUSAL-TEST -> MECHANISM -> HONEST-CAVEAT ladder. The T5b caveat rung is MANDATORY, not optional: the bank does not oversell a live hypothesis, and admitting the limits is itself the science lesson. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Strachan's 1989 BMJ paper used the 1958 British birth cohort (the National Child Development Study, roughly 17,000 children born in one week of March 1958). Some summaries — including one paragraph of Grokipedia's own article — wrongly say the 1970 cohort. The build MUST use 1958 and must verify the exact hay-fever percentages before putting any number in a stem. (2) NEVER write a rung as 'being dirty prevents allergies'. Strachan explicitly rejected that reading; the fact is microbial EXPOSURE, and ordinary hygiene still prevents dangerous infection. A rung that a parent could misread as 'stop washing your hands' is a failed rung. (3) The NEJM abstract states 4x and 6x — use the ratios, not invented percentages, unless the build sources them. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival explanations seriously proposed for the allergy rise — diesel particulates and air pollution, indoor dust mites and sealed houses, changed diet, better diagnosis and reporting, genetics. All were live; that is what makes them fair distractors. Dinner-test payoff: T3 — two farming communities that are almost the same people, one keeps its kids in the barn, and the barn kids do not get asthma. LANE BORDER: the Amish and Hutterites as CULTURES belong to HISTORY/GEOGRAPHY; every rung here must be keyed to the immune measurement, not to the way of life.

name: The forgotten organ: counting the hidden half
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: The microbes you carry — first seen in a man's own mouth, miscounted for forty years, and finally proved to be doing a job. T1: Delft, the 1670s and 80s. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth merchant who ground his own lenses, scraped the film off his own teeth, put it under a single-lens microscope of his own making and watched living things swimming about in it, some darting through the water like a pike. He wrote to the Royal Society that there were more living creatures in the scurf of one man's teeth than there were people in a whole kingdom. The first human being to see the hidden half found it in his own mouth — and you can repeat the experiment. T2: the number everybody quotes is wrong, and HOW it got fixed is the real lesson. 'You are ten times more bacteria than human' traces back to a single back-of-the-envelope estimate made in 1972 that nobody rechecked for four decades, while it was repeated in textbooks and lectures as though it had been measured. T3: in 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo actually did the arithmetic, organ by organ: about 3.8 x 10^13 bacterial cells against about 3.0 x 10^13 human cells — a ratio near one to one, and they said in print that 1:1 should replace the 10:1 and 100:1 figures in the literature. Their driest detail: a single bowel movement removes a quarter to a third of your bacteria, so you can shift the ratio yourself in about a minute. T3b: the same count produced a second surprise — roughly seven in ten of 'your' cells are red blood cells, which carry no nucleus and no DNA at all. By cell count, most of you is a bag of oxygen carriers. T4: why it earns the word ORGAN. Ann O'Hara and Fergus Shanahan called the gut flora 'the forgotten organ' in 2006, because it does jobs no human cell does — fermenting the fibre your own enzymes cannot touch, making vitamin K and several B vitamins, holding pathogens out simply by occupying the ground, and training the gut's immune tissue. Its microbes contribute on the order of a hundred times more distinct genes than your own genome does, which is why they can run chemistry you cannot. T5 (how we know it is causal and not merely correlated): raise a mouse germ-free, in a sterile isolator, and it grows up wrong — a hugely enlarged caecum, an underdeveloped gut immune system, extra vitamin requirements, altered behaviour. Give it a defined community of microbes and much of that is corrected. The germ-free animal is the control group that turns a correlation into a cause, and it is the single most important tool in the field. T5b (the open mystery, told honestly): the gut-brain claims are where the line has to be drawn. Germ-free mice really do behave differently, and there is strong evidence linking the mouse microbiome to brain development — but the leap from 'mouse behaviour changes' to 'your gut bacteria set your mood' is not established in humans, and the bank says so rather than pretending.
source: Sender R, Fuchs S, Milo R, 'Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body', PLoS Biology 2016 (B/H about 1.3, 'of the same order'; 3.8x10^13 bacteria vs 3.0x10^13 human cells; 'This B/H value of about 1:1 ... should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature'; red cells about 70 per cent of human cell count and the haematopoietic lineage 90 per cent; the old figure traced to a single 1972 back-of-the-envelope estimate; one defecation reducing bacterial content by a quarter to a third); Wikipedia 'Human microbiome' (about 38 trillion bacterial cells vs 30-40 trillion human cells; about 2 million bacterial genes against roughly 20,000 human genes); Wikipedia 'Germ-free animal' (defects in the immune system and in energy acquisition; strong evidence for microbiome-brain development interactions; germ-free animals used routinely to establish causality); Wikipedia 'Antonie van Leeuwenhoek' (single-lens microscopes magnifying up to about 275x, possibly 500x; over 500 lenses and at least 25 microscopes, nine surviving; found animalcules 'in rotten water, in ditches, on his own teeth'; described periodontitis; about 560 letters to the Royal Society). NOTE: the exact wording and date of the teeth letter (traditionally the 17 September 1683 letter) could NOT be verified this session — see accuracy rail.
framing_note: The keystone MECHANISM ladder of the 'hidden half', built around a CORRECTED-MISCONCEPTION rung that is on-voice gold: a wrong number survived forty years because it was repeated rather than checked, which IS the Feynman lesson about fooling yourself. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) The correction is roughly one-to-one (about 1.3:1) — NOT 'you are mostly bacteria'. Do not overcorrect into a second myth; the honest headline is 'about as many of them as of you'. (2) Leeuwenhoek's teeth letter must be verified against the published letters before ANY quotation marks are used. If the build cannot source the exact wording, paraphrase it and drop the quote — a documented quote or none. (3) On gut-brain, say 'no one yet knows' and make sure no distractor is secretly the answer. TEST-IT-YOURSELF: T1 is literally repeatable — a cheap microscope and a scraping — so frame it as an invitation, not a museum piece. DISTRACTOR MINE: real respectable-but-wrong claims — spontaneous generation, gut bacteria as harmless passengers doing nothing, 'all germs are harmful', and the 10:1 ratio itself, which is the best distractor in the ladder because it was in the textbooks. Dinner-test payoff: T3 — you can change your bacteria-to-human ratio by going to the bathroom. LANE BORDER: COOKING owns fermentation as food-making and probiotics as food; SCIENCE owns the counting, the germ-free control and the causal test.

name: The transplant that beat squeamishness
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: Clostridioides difficile, the disease you catch from the cure, and the treatment that had to defeat disgust before it could defeat the bug. T2: C. diff is caused by a VACANCY, not by an arrival. A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics clears out the gut's resident community; C. diff, present all along in small numbers, takes the empty ground, multiplies and releases toxins that strip the lining of the colon. The commonest trigger for the infection is the treatment for a different infection. T3: because the problem is a vacancy, the fix is to refill it. In November 1958 a Denver surgeon, Ben Eiseman, and colleagues treated four critically ill patients with fulminant pseudomembranous colitis using faecal enemas from healthy donors, and reported a rapid return to health in the journal Surgery. The idea then sat almost unused for fifty years — not because it failed, but because of disgust. T3b: it is far older than 1958. In fourth-century China, Ge Hong's handbook of emergency medicine recorded giving a preparation of human stool for severe diarrhoea and food poisoning, and in the sixteenth century Li Shizhen described a 'yellow soup' used the same way. T4 (the test that ended the argument): Els van Nood and colleagues in Amsterdam ran a proper randomised trial — donor faeces infused through a tube into the duodenum against standard vancomycin — and published it in the New England Journal of Medicine in January 2013. About 81 per cent were cured by a single infusion and over 90 per cent after a second; the antibiotic arm did far worse. The trial was STOPPED EARLY, because once the gap was that wide it was no longer defensible to keep assigning patients to the losing treatment. T5: it is now a licensed medicine rather than a folk remedy — the FDA approved Rebyota, given rectally, in December 2022, and Vowst, an oral capsule of purified bacterial spores, in April 2023: the first stool-derived products approved as drugs. The whole journey from repulsive to prescribable ran through one controlled trial. T5b (the honest caveat and the open question): FMT works spectacularly for recurrent C. diff and much less clearly for the many other conditions it has been tried on; donor screening genuinely matters, because transmitted organisms have caused serious harm; and nobody can yet say WHICH microbes do the work — which is precisely what the purified-spore products are an attempt to find out.
source: Wikipedia 'Fecal microbiota transplant' (Ge Hong, 4th century, Handbook of Emergency Medicine, donor faeces for food poisoning and diarrhoea; Li Shizhen, Ming dynasty, 'yellow soup'; Eiseman et al., Surgery, November 1958, four critically ill patients with fulminant pseudomembranous colitis treated by faecal enema with rapid return to health; van Nood et al., NEJM, January 2013, duodenal infusion, 81 per cent cured after a single infusion and over 90 per cent after a second, study stopped early for effectiveness; Rebyota approved December 2022, rectal; Vowst approved April 2023, first oral faecal microbiota product). NOTE: grokipedia.com could not be reached for the FMT page this session (shared browser session was clobbered) — the build's research stage must run the Grokipedia check on 'Fecal microbiota transplantation' and 'Clostridioides difficile' before authoring.
framing_note: This ladder is the sub-strand's proof that EVIDENCE can beat revulsion — the obstacle was an emotional reaction, and a randomised trial removed it. RAILS: (1) The stopped-early fact is the payoff and must be stated precisely: the trial was halted because continuing to assign patients to the losing arm was no longer justifiable, NOT because FMT harmed anyone. Getting this backwards would invert the lesson. (2) Use 'about 81 per cent after a single infusion' only as sourced to van Nood et al. 2013 — do not round it into a slogan or attach it to conditions other than recurrent C. diff. (3) Do not present FMT as a general cure-all; the T5b caveat rung is required. TONE: clinical and matter-of-fact throughout — the subject is funny to a ten-year-old and the bank must not wink at it. NEVER a joke option; the humour, if any, is in the reality, not the writing. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real losing treatments and rival explanations — repeated vancomycin courses, over-the-counter probiotic yoghurt, 'wait it out', surgery to remove the colon, and the older belief that C. diff was simply an antibiotic-resistant superbug rather than an opportunist filling a vacancy. Dinner-test payoff: T4. LANE BORDER: COOKING owns fermented foods and probiotics as food; SCIENCE owns the trial, the vacancy mechanism and the licensing.

name: Fever is a weapon, not a malfunction
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: A corrected misconception, tested on an animal that cannot run a fever by itself. T2: 1975 — Matthew Kluger, David Ringler and Melvin Anver infected desert iguanas with the bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila. A lizard cannot heat itself from the inside; if it wants to be warmer it has to go and find heat. The infected lizards deliberately moved to hotter places and pushed their body temperature up — and the ones allowed to do it survived far better than the ones held cool. Their paper in Science on 11 April 1975 was titled, flatly, 'Fever and survival'. T3: the reptile IS the experiment. In a mammal you cannot separate the fever from the infection that produced it — they arrive together. In a lizard the experimenter controls the temperature from outside, so temperature becomes the variable and survival becomes the readout. That is what turns an observation into a test, and it is the reason a lizard answered a question about you. T4 (mechanism): fever is not the infection overheating you. It is your own hypothalamus deliberately MOVING ITS TARGET. Pyrogens released during infection drive production of prostaglandin E2 in the brain, the set point rises, and your body then shivers and shuts down blood flow to the skin in order to climb to the new setting. That is why you feel freezing cold while your temperature is climbing — the chill is the ascent, not the illness. T4b: aspirin and ibuprofen do not cool you directly; they block the enzymes that make prostaglandin E2, which lowers the set point, after which your body sheds the heat by itself. T5 (the honest open question): if fever helps, should it be suppressed? The human evidence is genuinely mixed — large trials in critically ill patients have not shown that routine fever control improves survival, and have not shown clear harm either. The bank's position is that this is unsettled. The misconception worth killing is narrower and firmer: 'my temperature is up, therefore my thermostat is broken'. The thermostat is working exactly as designed.
source: Kluger MJ, Ringler DH, Anver MR, 'Fever and survival', Science 1975 Apr 11;188(4184):166-8 (desert lizards Dipsosaurus dorsalis infected with Aeromonas hydrophila, held at low 34-36C, neutral 38C or high 40-42C ambient temperatures; elevated temperature after experimental bacterial infection produced a significant increase in host survival); Wikipedia 'Fever' (pyrogens driving prostaglandin E2 action on the hypothalamic set point; fever thought to contribute to host defence by hindering pathogens with strict temperature requirements; warm-blooded vertebrates recovering more rapidly from infection with fever; and the counterweight that in humans 'treating a fever does not appear to improve or worsen outcomes', with no mortality benefit found in sepsis or critical-illness trials).
framing_note: A CORRECTED-MISCONCEPTION plus MECHANISM ladder — the misconception being killed is 'fever is damage'. RAILS: (1) Never turn T5 into medical advice about whether to take a fever reducer. State what the trials found and stop; this is a quiz bank, not a clinic. (2) Kluger's lizards raised their temperature BEHAVIOURALLY by moving to warmer ground — do not write it as a lizard 'getting a fever' the way a mammal does; that distinction is the whole methodological point. (3) Very high fevers ARE dangerous and the ladder must never imply otherwise. (4) Kluger's exact survival percentages were not retrievable this session — the direction of the result is sourced; specific numbers must be verified in the 1975 paper before appearing in a stem. DISTRACTOR MINE: real ideas serious doctors held — fever as pure pathology to be broken at all costs, fever as the body 'burning off' toxins, the humoral heat imbalance, and the modern half-truth that fever merely means 'you are fighting something' without any mechanism. Dinner-test payoff: T4 — you shiver and feel freezing precisely BECAUSE your thermostat has been reset upward, and the chill is you climbing toward the new setting. LANE BORDER: reptile basking and thermoregulation as natural history belong to the ANIMAL bank; here the iguana is an instrument and the tested fact is the METHOD.
history_overlap: ANIMAL bank may cover reptile basking and ectotherm thermoregulation as behaviour — this ladder must key the EXPERIMENT (external temperature as the controlled variable, survival as the readout), never iguana natural history.

name: The second dose that killed: anaphylaxis on the Prince's yacht
strand: The immune system & the hidden half
scope: A mini gem: the experiment that produced the exact opposite of what it was designed to produce, and was reported anyway. T3: in 1901 Paul Portier and Charles Richet were guests aboard Prince Albert I of Monaco's research yacht, the Princesse Alice II, trying to make dogs RESISTANT to the sting of the Portuguese man o' war by giving them small doses of the toxin — the same logic of graded exposure that had already worked for other poisons. It failed in the most surprising way available. T4: dogs that had shrugged off a first injection weeks earlier collapsed and died within minutes of a SECOND, much smaller dose. Richet coined 'aphylaxis' — without protection — then changed it to 'anaphylaxis' because he preferred the sound; he and Portier announced it to the Societe de Biologie in Paris on 15 February 1902, and Richet received the 1913 Nobel Prize for it. T5: the wonder is what it reveals about immune memory. Memory is not automatically protective. The very machinery that makes a second exposure harmless can, aimed slightly differently, make a second exposure lethal — which is why a person can eat peanuts for a decade and then nearly die of one, and why the modern rescue drug, adrenaline, treats the REACTION rather than the allergen.
source: Wikipedia 'Charles Richet' (1901 voyage with Paul Portier aboard Prince Albert I of Monaco's Princesse Alice II; toxins extracted from cnidarians — Portuguese man o' war and the sea anemone Actinia sulcata; dogs tolerated the first injection but developed fatal shock on subsequent injection about three weeks later; 'aphylaxis' coined in 1902 and changed to 'anaphylaxis' for euphony, from the Greek for 'against protection'; findings presented to the Societe de Biologie in Paris on 15 February 1902; 1913 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the work on anaphylaxis).
framing_note: A MINI REVERSAL gem — the hook is that they were trying to create PROTECTION and created its opposite, and published it rather than burying it. RAILS: (1) The intention is the load-bearing fact; a stem that starts from 'they were studying allergy' destroys the rung. (2) The famous dog 'Neptune' belongs to the Paris follow-up rather than the yacht in most accounts — the build must NOT put the dog's name, or the exact location of the fatal second dose, in the tested slot unless it can source it; the yacht voyage (1901) and the Paris announcement (Feb 1902) are the safe anchors. (3) Anaphylaxis kills children; the tone stays serious and there are no joke options. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real adjacent science where graded or repeated dosing DID work or was believed to — Behring's diphtheria antitoxin, Pasteur's attenuated cultures, Mithridates' legendary poison tolerance told AS legend, and von Pirquet and Schick's serum sickness (they coined 'allergy' in 1906), which is the closest true neighbour. Dinner-test payoff: T4 — the smaller, second dose was the one that killed. LANE BORDER: none; keep the man o' war as a toxin source, not as ANIMAL-bank natural history.
